Grant such order, further relief(s) in the facts and circumstances of the case as this Commission may deem just and equitable in favour of the Petitioner._ ” 3. Brief facts necessary to appreciate the issues in the present case, as noted in the Petition, are as under: 4. The Commission admitted the Petition on 29.7.2022, and the notice was issued to the parties for filing their respective replies. In compliance with such directions, the Respondents, UPPCL and TPTCL, filed their replies to the Petition on 16.8.2022 and 22.8.2022, respectively. The Petitioner has also filed its rejoinders to the replies filed by UPPCL and TPTCL. (a) The claim of the Respondent UPPCL that the Petitioner has suppressed its contractual arrangement is misplaced, as the Commission, in its order dated 17.9.2018, had already considered and acknowledged the back-to-back nature of the arrangement involving the Petitioner, TPTCL, and UPPCL. The Commission, in the aforementioned order, has held that a binding contractual relationship existed based on the LoIs and recognized the nexus between the Petitioner and UPPCL, notwithstanding the intermediary role of TPTCL. 15. The Petition was heard on 28.1.2025, and the order was reserved in the matter. Based on the request of the learned counsels for the parties, the Petitioner and the Respondents were permitted to file their respective written submissions. Accordingly, the parties have filed their respective written submissions, which are not repeated here for the sake of brevity and reiteration. **_Issue No. 1: Whether the claim raised by the Petitioner in the present Petition is barred by the principles of constructive res judicata as well as Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?_** 18. Although the RfP dated 22.12.2015 in the present case contains an arbitration clause, the prayer(s) of the Petitioner seeking the payment of LPS in this Petition is nothing but a consequential relief, upon UPPCL making the Change in Law compensation payment to the Petitioner in terms of the order dated 17.9.2018 passed by this Commission in Petition No. 158/MP/2017. Hence, in line with the findings of the Commission in the above case, the dispute involved is not referable to ‘arbitration’ and the same is to be adjudicated by the Commission under Section 79 of the Act. In light of the above, we now proceed to deal with the issues outlined earlier. # **Issue No. 1: Whether the claim raised by the Petitioner in the present Petition is barred by the principles of constructive res judicata as well as Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?** 21. We have considered the submissions of both parties. We note that the gravamen of the Petitioner emanates from the delay in honouring the invoices by the Respondent UPPCL in light of the order passed in Petition No. 158/MP/2017. According to the Respondent, UPPCL carrying cost, and the LPS claimed by the Petitioner in the present Petition are not maintainable in view of provisions of Order II Rule 2 of the CPC and also in light of constructive _res-judicata_ under Section 11 of the CPC. The Respondent UPPCL has submitted that since the Petitioner omitted to claim LPS in the main Petition, the Petitioner cannot be allowed to file a subsequent Petition to claim the relief so omitted. On the other hand, the Petitioner has submitted that the issue raised is squarely covered by the Commission’s decision dated 9.8.2023 in Petition No. 173/MP/2022, wherein a similar objection was raised and rejected by the Commission. It has also been submitted by the Petitioner that since the entitlement of LPS arose upon delay in payment made by Respondent UPPCL, the same claim could not have been raised in the original Change in Law Petition No. 158/MP/2017. _“11. Res judicata— No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court._ _Explanation III.—The matter above referred to must in the former suit have been alleged by one party and either denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other._ 27. In the present case, the claim of the Petitioner for the LPS on the Change in Law compensation is premised on an entirely different and distinct cause of action than its claim for the Change in Law compensation. The former is premised on the Respondent UPPCL having failed to honour the invoices raised towards the Change in Law compensation and cannot said to be a ground of attack/claim that is essentially connected with or incidental to the Change in Law determination as involved in earlier Petition No. 158/MP/2017 filed by the Petitioner. Also, the Commission in its order dated 9.8.2023 in Petition No. 173/MP/2022 has observed that the “right to sue” in relation to LPS claims can begin to run only when there is a default in making the payment of LPS, which can only be subsequent to the crystallization of the LPS liability, i.e. date on which the payment towards the invoices has been made. In view of the same, in the present case, the Petitioner could not have claimed the same in the original Petition No. 158/MP/2017, as the Petitioner’s right to claim LPS crystallized only upon the payment of the principal amount by Respondent UPPCL, i.e., on 24.5.2021. Therefore, the contention of the Respondent that the present Petition is barred by constructive _res judicata_ and Order II Rule 2 is not tenable. to agree with the contentions of the Respondent UPPCL that the Petitioner has suppressed material facts with respect to its contractual relationships.
